title: A secret key that browsers trusted to vouch for websites was the number 4
body: On 17 October 2026 a researcher reported that eight intermediate certificates of the Indian certificate authority eMudhra had private keys anyone could work out, and within three days Chrome, Firefox, Apple and Microsoft had blocked them. When your browser shows a padlock, the site’s certificate is signed by an intermediate, which is signed by a root built into the browser. Each signature needs a private key: for the curve P-384, a whole number picked at random, up to **116 digits** long. The public key comes from adding a starting point on the curve to itself that many times, which is quick, but nobody knows a fast way back, so finding the key means searching an unthinkable number of possibilities. eMudhra’s keys were all below 256, and one was simply 4, so trying the first 256 numbers found them in under a second, as [Mozilla’s incident report](https://bugzilla.mozilla.org/show_bug.cgi?id=2083449) explains. With them, anyone could have issued fake certificates for websites they don’t control. eMudhra said a faulty script had made weak keys with look-alike labels at a key ceremony in April 2025, and that staff picked the wrong ones.

slides.question: Keys for P-384, an elliptic curve used to sign web certificates, are random whole numbers. Up to how many digits?
slides.explanation: 116. Keys are picked from 1 up to about 3.9 × 10¹¹⁵, the number of points on the curve. Each of the eight weak keys at the Indian certificate authority eMudhra had three digits at most.

slides.alt: Animation on midnight blue: a browser padlock and a chain of three cream certificates with red seals. A toy curve of teal dots hops G, 2G, 3G; a 116-digit key; squares for the digits of the years a search would take. Then all 256 small keys light up eMudhra’s eight, a fake certificate, BLOCKED.
slides.music: “Goblin Tinker Soldier Spy” Kevin MacLeod (incompetech.com) · CC BY 4.0

slides.prompt: Run the search, then lengthen the key until trying every one, at a trillion a second, would outlast the universe.
slides.takeaway: From 99 bits, trying every key outlasts the universe. eMudhra’s keys had 8 bits of choice; a real P-384 key has 384, so even cleverer attacks are hopeless.

slides.heading: Did a fake get through?
slides.text: Chrome rejects website certificates that aren’t listed in public Certificate Transparency logs. It found none signed by eMudhra’s six weak web intermediates before it blocked them, so no fake made with them could have fooled Chrome by default. The worry is apps and devices that never learn a certificate was revoked.

events.text: eMudhra makes a batch of 24 keys
Weak keys reported; Chrome and Firefox block them
eMudhra says it will leave the global web-certificate business

slides.question: Why did a weak key at eMudhra put any website at risk, not just eMudhra’s customers?
options: It could sign for any site name
It unlocked the browsers’ root keys
It decrypted all past web traffic
slides.explanation: A trusted intermediate can sign a certificate for any website, and browsers accept it because it chains up to a root they trust. That is why the keys had to be blocked everywhere at once.

source.label: Mozilla Security Blog: Protecting Firefox users following the compromise of eMudhra intermediate certificates
